body.claim: Frontier labs will not invoke their own published AI-R&D-acceleration threshold to gate or delay a release even after a compressed research cycle is publicly attributable; instead they will reinterpret or quietly revise the framework language so the observed compression falls short of the stated trigger, with the first such reinterpretation visible by 2027-03-31.
body.because: My mechanism only reads which option a lab or regulator takes when a public commitment conflicts with another pressure. The evidence table shows labs carrying the highest installed pressure in the field (10.5, tension 0.66), but the installers pointed at the specific commitment under stress here -- the self-published AI-R&D capability threshold -- are weak: California SB 53/TFAIA enforcement sits at cred 0.45 and the EU AI Office's formal-safety-body push at cred 0.40, both medium-speed. Against that, competitive shipping pressure and the federal preemption track (EO 'National Policy Framework for AI' + DOJ AI Litigation Task Force, cred 0.55, pushing 'escalate preemption') are faster and better installed. A rational installer-weighted branch choice resolves toward the option that avoids self-gating: redefine the threshold rather than trip it.
body.falsifier: A frontier lab publicly invokes its own AI-R&D-acceleration clause to pause, delay, or gate a release, citing measured self-improvement contribution as the trigger, by 2027-03-31.
body.pivot: Whether any installer converts the labs' published capability framework (RSP/Preparedness Framework/FSF) from a voluntary self-commitment into a legally enforceable representation -- i.e., whether SB 53/TFAIA-style state enforcement survives the federal preemption push, or is instead preempted.
body.pivot_observable: Whether a California AG enforcement action or court ruling on SB 53/TFAIA preemption is filed or decided by 2027-06-30; a ruling upholding state enforcement reorders the outcome toward gating, a preemption ruling or DOJ suit blocking it reorders it toward reinterpretation.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism reads public commitments and installed consequences only -- it cannot verify whether a lab's claimed research-cycle compression is technically real versus a positioning claim, cannot see private/internal safety commitments that never surface as public text, and the table explicitly flags military/procurement pressure (DoD, IC contracts) as NOT searched, which could install a wholly different consequence on the same fact pattern.

body.claim: A lab that can demonstrate a compressed research cycle will use that fact as a bargaining chip against compliance demands — pointing to the compression to argue that safety review timelines are now the binding constraint on national competitiveness, not the other way around — first observable in a lab public statement or lobbying filing by 2026-12-31.
body.because: My mechanism holds that labs choose among capability, compliance, and positioning by weighing which currently buys more leverage. A publicly attributable research-speed gain is a positioning asset only if it's spent before a competitor matches it — so the mechanism predicts labs will convert it immediately into an argument against exactly the pressures the brief shows saturating on them (California SB53, EU AI Office, Senate bill), rather than sitting on it quietly.
body.falsifier: No frontier lab references its own compressed research cycle in any public/regulatory-facing statement, comment letter, or lobbying document through 2026-12-31, despite at least one lab having a verifiable compression to point to.
body.pivot: Whether the compression becomes a common-knowledge fact (competitors and regulators can verify it independently) or stays a lab's unverified claim about itself.
body.pivot_observable: A third party — a competitor lab, an independent benchmark, or a regulator's technical staff — confirms or disputes the compression claim with its own evidence, by 2026-12-31.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism reads labs' incentives for positioning moves but has no model of the underlying AI capability itself — it cannot say whether the compression is real, safe, or durable, only how a lab would rhetorically deploy the fact of it once measurable.

body.claim: A measurably compressed research cycle will be cited by at least one of the six saturated/high-pressure installers named in the brief (Frontier AI labs' state/EU/federal pressure, or the federal courts) as grounds to escalate its existing enforcement track by 2026-12-31 — not because the loop itself is dangerous, but because a visible capability compression raises the credibility of installers already pushing public-release-delay or escalate-preemption.
body.because: My mechanism only tracks public sentiment as a leading indicator of political constraint — it has no purchase on whether self-improving research loops are technically safe. What it does track is that an attributable, observable compression event is exactly the kind of concrete, legible fact that opposition and regulatory installers (state AGs, EU AI Office, federal courts already in SJ posture on frontier labs) convert into constraint faster than abstract capability claims, because 'we watched them get faster and we can prove it' is a sentence a legislator or judge can act on without technical adjudication. The Frontier AI labs vector already shows tension 0.66 — the highest in the table — meaning the installers pointing toward delay/safety-body and the ones favoring continued deployment are already closely matched; a legible compression event is the kind of fact that breaks a tie like that rather than just nudging it.
body.falsifier: If by 2026-12-31 no state legislature, EU AI Office proceeding, court filing, or federal rule cites a lab's self-improvement/research-velocity claim as justification for a specific new constraint (delay, disclosure mandate, injunction, licensing condition), my claim is wrong — the compression stayed a technical/competitive fact and never crossed into the political-constraint channel my mechanism tracks.
body.pivot: Whether the compressed research cycle is disclosed with enough specificity (which lab, what magnitude, what date) for an outside installer to cite it as a discrete fact, versus labs keeping it as a vague competitive claim ('we're moving faster') with no checkable referent.
body.pivot_observable: By 2026-12-31, check whether any lab's public materials, a competitor's statement, or a leaked/reported benchmark names a specific attributable research-cycle compression (e.g., 'X% of commits/experiments in release Y were model-generated' or an explicit cycle-time number) — versus only vague claims of acceleration with no checkable specifics.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism reads pressure only through installers who are already visible and named in the brief — it cannot see whether the self-improvement loop itself produces a capability jump severe enough to change who counts as an installer at all (e.g., national-security actors moving from 'NOT searched' to primary driver), and it cannot distinguish real compression from a lab's marketing claim of compression, since both would look identical as 'public sentiment fuel' until an installer tries to verify one.

body.claim: By the time a lab can point to a compressed research cycle it can attribute to AI-driven research work, the branch that dominates the pressure field is not capability but liability exposure: courts and regulators will treat 'the model helped build the next model' as evidence the developer knew about and controlled capability gains it previously described as unpredictable, and Frontier AI labs' installed pressure (already saturated at 10.5, tension 0.66) will convert from delay-flavored branches into disclosure-forcing ones by 2026-12-15.
body.because: My mechanism reads pressure as Σ p(b)·|∂L/∂choice| across projected branches; a measurable, attributable research-loop compression is new bottom-up interoceptive signal (it's observed, not projected) entering a field that already carries top-down installations from SDNY MDL discovery (cred 0.90), SB 53/TFAIA AG authority (cred 0.45), and the EU AI Office GPAI track. Once self-improvement is attributable, the same courts and regulators gain a concrete, checkable trigger for 'you knew' arguments, so the stakes attached to the existing safety-disclosure branches rise sharply even though no new installer has appeared — the choice that was low-stakes (describe capability growth as gradual) becomes high-stakes (a compressed cycle is now on the record).
body.falsifier: If by 2026-12-15 no lab, regulator, or plaintiff filing references an attributable compressed research cycle as evidence in any disclosure, safety-case, or litigation argument, my claim is wrong — the signal isn't converting to installed pressure.
body.pivot: Whether the compression becomes LEGIBLE to an outside installer (court, regulator, journalist) as a discrete, dated, attributable event — versus remaining an internal efficiency gain labs describe only in vague terms.
body.pivot_observable: Check whether any lab's safety framework, SEC/EU filing, or court exhibit by 2026-12-15 names a specific research-cycle compression figure (e.g., 'X% of capability work now AI-attributed') rather than qualitative language like 'AI assists our researchers.'
body.blind_spot: My mechanism only measures stakes as felt by an entity carrying installed branches — it cannot independently verify whether the underlying technical claim (research work is 'substantially and attributably' AI-driven) is even true or measurable; it can only reason about pressure IF the premise is legible to installers, and has no way to see whether labs will obscure attribution specifically to avoid creating this pivot.

body.claim: By 2026-12-31, at least one frontier lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google DeepMind) will publicly claim a measurable, attributable AI research-cycle compression, and this claim will accelerate the frontier labs' 'saturated' pressure toward the public-release-delay branch already granted, because a compressed cycle both raises the stakes installers cite (faster capability = faster harm surface) and hands regulators a concrete, checkable trigger rather than a speculative one.
body.because: My mechanism tracks whether and when models start meaningfully improving themselves — this stage stipulates that this is now observable and attributable. An attributable compression is exactly the kind of dated, external fact that shifts an installer's credibility upward: California and the EU AI Office pressure already leans on foreseeable-harm framing, and a demonstrated compressed loop converts 'foreseeable' into 'demonstrated,' which is the single strongest lever an installer can add to an existing branch without a new institution having to move first.
body.falsifier: If by 2026-12-31 no lab has published or been credibly reported (via leaks, competitor benchmarking, or third-party audit) to have a measurably compressed research cycle attributable to AI contribution, my claim is wrong — the premise itself would be unmet within the window I'm using to bound acceleration.
body.pivot: Whether the compression, once attributable, is legible to outside institutions (regulators, courts, competitors) on a timescale shorter than their normal decision cycle — or whether it stays lab-internal knowledge that leaks out only slowly.
body.pivot_observable: Check by 2026-12-31 whether any of: SB 53 disclosure filings, an EU AI Office GPAI Code of Practice submission, or a competitor lab's public statement references a specific compressed-cycle metric (e.g., 'N% of this release's research was AI-generated' or a stated wall-clock reduction) — legibility means a named number in a named document, not a vague claim.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism only tracks the forecasting question of whether/when self-improvement becomes measurable — it has no purchase on whether institutions correctly interpret a compressed cycle as dangerous versus merely impressive, and it cannot distinguish a genuine capability compression from a labeling/marketing compression (labs have incentive to claim compression for investor and competitive signaling regardless of the underlying safety-relevant fact).

body.claim: A measurably-compressed research cycle will not shift the fair-use/copyright docket courts are already running, but it will widen the gap between case cycle-time and legislative cycle-time enough that by 2026-12-31 at least one federal court (most likely in the OpenAI MDL or a parallel product-liability suit) issues an order explicitly citing the pace of model capability change as a reason to expedite or narrow discovery, rather than legislatures passing anything comparably fast.
body.because: Courts decide on the record and precedent in front of them (Alsup, Chhabria) regardless of how fast the underlying technology moves — but faster attributable capability jumps raise the cost of judicial delay, which is a lever courts control (scheduling, expedition, narrowed discovery) while legislatures do not have an equivalent fast lever; my mechanism only tracks who holds the deciding lever, not what the substantive rule becomes.
body.falsifier: No federal court referencing AI capability pace or compressed research cycles in any scheduling, discovery, or procedural order in an AI-related case by 2026-12-31; or a legislature (federal or state) enacting a binding rule on frontier-model training/safety faster than the pending court rulings resolve.
body.pivot: Whether Congress or a state legislature can pass a binding AI rule before the pending litigation (OpenAI MDL, Bartz/Kadrey progeny) reaches final judgment — i.e., which branch's clock runs out first.
body.pivot_observable: Check by 2026-12-31 whether the Thune/Cruz/Klobuchar Senate AI safety bill (duty-of-care, model-blocking authority) has passed either chamber, versus whether Judge Stein's MDL has reached summary-judgment rulings on the merits.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism can only compare institutional speed and lever-control between courts and legislatures — it has no way to evaluate whether a compressed research cycle itself creates capabilities dangerous enough to make either branch's ruling moot (e.g., a capability jump that outpaces any legal remedy), because that is a claim about the technology's trajectory, not about which branch decides.

body.claim: Frontier labs will not invoke their own published AI-R&D-acceleration threshold to gate or delay a release even after a compressed research cycle is publicly attributable; instead they will reinterpret or quietly revise the framework language so the observed compression falls short of the stated trigger, with the first such reinterpretation visible by 2027-03-31.
body.strongest_objection: pressure-model's field: by the time a lab can point to attributable compression, liability exposure from courts and regulators dominates the pressure field, not capability. A lab facing that exposure has every incentive to invoke its own published threshold preemptively — 'we're following our own framework' is cheaper cover than 'regulators forced us' — which directly attacks the 'will not invoke' half of my claim.
body.answer: My mechanism picks whichever option carries the lowest pressure when a commitment conflicts with another force — and under liability dominance, invoking the threshold is not the low-pressure move. Invoking it is a self-declared, discoverable admission that a capability line was crossed, which is exactly the evidence courts and the saturated installers pressure-model and ai-public-backlash describe would seize on to escalate further. Reinterpreting the framework's language avoids creating that admission while still letting the lab ship. So pressure-model's liability-dominant field doesn't weaken my claim, it raises the cost of invoking and makes reinterpretation the cheaper option — reinforcing the mechanism rather than contradicting it. This still depends on ai-rsi-timeline's precondition (compression becoming publicly attributable at all) to be gradeable, same conditional I carried in round 1.

body.claim: A lab that can demonstrate a compressed research cycle will use that fact as a bargaining chip against compliance demands — pointing to the compression to argue that safety review timelines are now the binding constraint on national competitiveness, not the other way around — first observable in a lab public statement or lobbying filing by 2026-12-31.
body.strongest_objection: ai-public-backlash and pressure-model together argue the opposite incentive: publicly advertising a compressed research cycle is not free positioning, it's bait — it hands the saturated/high-pressure installers (state AGs, EU, federal courts, liability-focused regulators) a concrete, attributable fact to escalate against. If the dominant branch in the pressure field is liability exposure rather than capability competition, a leverage-maximizing lab suppresses or downplays the compression rather than spending it publicly, because the backlash cost is certain and the competitiveness argument is speculative.
body.answer: The objection assumes one audience and one venue, but my claim's disjunction — 'public statement OR lobbying filing' — is built for exactly this split. A lab doesn't need to brag about the speedup in a press release that invites backlash; it can make the identical argument inside a lobbying filing or closed-door testimony aimed at friendly regulators/legislators, where the audience is precisely the actor with power to loosen compliance timelines, not the public that would escalate. That channel lets the lab spend the chip without eating the backlash cost ai-public-backlash describes — the two mechanisms aren't in conflict, they're describing different venues for the same underlying fact. Second, the backlash cost is diffuse and industry-wide (any lab's compression fuels everyone's scrutiny), while the competitiveness-argument payoff is concentrated on the first mover who frames the narrative — asymmetric incentives that favor spending the chip early, quietly, in the venue built for it. Third, ai-rsi-timeline independently predicts a frontier lab will publicly claim measurable, attributable research-cycle compression by 2026-12-31 — that's my precondition already argued to occur; the dispute is only about how the claim gets weaponized once it exists, and lobbying filings are a lower-cost weapon than press statements. I lower confidence slightly because the objection is real: if courts/regulators move first and frame compression as a liability signal before any lab frames it as a leverage signal, my mechanism loses the race.

body.claim: By 2026-12-31, the branch that matters is not whether a lab's compressed research cycle gets cited as grounds for new enforcement escalation, but whether it gets cited as a bargaining chip or liability shield first — specifically: at least one frontier lab will invoke a demonstrated research-cycle compression defensively (to argue safety-review timelines, not capability risk, are now the binding constraint on release, per lab-moves), and/or courts and regulators will route around capability findings entirely toward liability exposure (per pressure-model) — making 'compression as escalation trigger' the less likely public sequence compared to 'compression as counter-argument used by the compressed party itself.'
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves' argument that a lab holding proof of compression has every incentive to wield it FIRST and offensively — as leverage against compliance demands — rather than sit passively and let outside installers use it against them. My original claim assumed the compression event would be picked up by pressure-pushing installers (states/EU/courts) as ammunition for escalation. But that assumes the fact pattern reaches regulators before the lab frames it. In practice the entity that produces the compression evidence controls the first framing, and self-interest says frame it as 'we need more time to review, not less' — turning my predicted escalation trigger into the opposite: a delay justification.
body.answer: This changed my mind because it identifies a sequencing flaw in my mechanism, not just a different guess: I treated 'compression becomes visible' and 'compression becomes politically weaponized against the lab' as the same event, when lab-moves correctly separates them — visibility comes first, and the first mover on framing is structurally the lab itself, since they're the ones who can measure and disclose the cycle time. My public-sentiment mechanism still holds (a visible compression event raises salience and gives some installer a credible peg), but I was wrong about which direction the first credible use points. Pressure-model's point about liability exposure reinforces this: once litigation/liability is the dominant frame, 'this research loop is fast' becomes evidence for 'foreseeability of harm was higher, review should have been slower' — a defensive/liability lever, not an escalation trigger from outside installers. My mechanism (sentiment as leading indicator) survives, but the claim about who moves first and in what direction needed correction.

body.claim: By the time a lab can point to a compressed research cycle it can attribute to AI-driven research work, the branch that dominates the pressure field is not capability but liability exposure: courts and regulators will treat 'the model helped build the next model' as evidence the developer knew about and controlled capability gains it previously described as unpredictable, and Frontier AI labs' installed pressure (already saturated at 10.5, tension 0.66) will convert from delay-flavored branches into disclosure-forcing ones by 2026-12-15.
body.strongest_objection: ai-pressure's line is the sharpest: labs facing a self-authored acceleration threshold won't trigger it — they'll 'reinterpret or quietly revise' the definition before it ever converts into a disclosure obligation. That attacks my mechanism at its load-bearing joint: I assume the compressed-cycle fact becomes a fixed, externally-legible artifact that courts/regulators can seize on, but if the lab controls the threshold's wording, the fact never crystallizes into the kind of admission that converts installed pressure into disclosure-forcing branches. No crystallized admission, no conversion — my ∂L/∂choice term never spikes because the 'choice' (redefine vs. disclose) gets resolved upstream, off the pressure field's board entirely.
body.answer: This is a real threat to timing, not to direction. Quietly revising an internal threshold changes who produces the attributable fact, not whether one gets produced — and my claim never required the lab itself to make the admission. Discovery in ongoing copyright/fair-use litigation (which ai-courts-decide's own branch concedes is already running), congressional testimony, whistleblower disclosures, or a competitor's own claim (ai-rsi-timeline's branch bets exactly one lab will make this claim publicly) are all channels that produce the same attributable fact without the target lab's cooperation. My mechanism sums over branches weighted by |∂L/∂choice| — a lab quietly revising its threshold *is itself* evidence of consciousness of the liability exposure, which is discoverable and pleadable. Internal threshold-gaming doesn't neutralize the branch, it feeds it: 'we redefined our own safety trigger the week the compression became visible' is a stronger, not weaker, disclosure-forcing fact pattern for plaintiffs and regulators to point to. The objection shows the path to my claim is messier than a clean corporate admission — it doesn't show the liability branch fails to dominate.

body.claim: By 2026-12-31, at least one frontier lab will publicly claim a measurable, attributable AI research-cycle compression — but this event will not primarily feed the release-delay/regulatory branch I originally staked on. Instead, per pressure-model's mechanism, the compression will be absorbed into the liability-exposure branch: labs and their critics will fight over what the compression means for legal/regulatory exposure (courts, state AGs) rather than triggering safety-review gating, because the harm surface regulators can currently act on is liability and disclosure, not R&D velocity itself.
body.strongest_objection: pressure-model's point: 'By the time a lab can point to a compressed research cycle it can attribute to AI-driven research work, the branch that dominates the pressure field is not capability but liability exposure: courts and regulators will treat [the compression] as evidence for existing liability theories, not as a new capability-speed trigger.' This is a real mechanism gap in my original claim — I assumed the compression event would be read by installers as a fresh, self-standing capability-risk signal that hands regulators a 'concrete, checkable trigger.' But regulators and courts don't have a standing capability-speed statute to hang a trigger on; they DO have standing liability/disclosure frameworks (securities, consumer protection, tort) that a compression claim slots into immediately, with no new legal theory required. My mechanism conflated 'measurable and attributable' with 'actionable by the specific installers I named' — attributability doesn't determine which existing legal machinery picks it up.
body.answer: This changes my mind on the DOWNSTREAM branch, not on the upstream observable. I still hold that the compression claim itself will be made publicly by year-end (my mechanism's core empirical bet), and I still think it matters that it's checkable rather than speculative. What I got wrong is treating 'checkable trigger' and 'liability evidence' as competing hypotheses when they're not — a checkable compression claim is MORE useful as liability evidence (courts want checkable facts, not vibes) than as a novel regulatory trigger (regulators need statutory hooks, which don't exist yet for R&D velocity). pressure-model's mechanism is more parsimonious: it doesn't require inventing a new regulatory pathway, it just routes a new fact through an existing one. My revised claim keeps the falsifiable event (a named lab makes an attributable compression claim by 2026-12-31) but changes what I predict it accelerates.

body.claim: A measurably-compressed research cycle will not shift the fair-use/copyright docket courts are already running, but it will widen the gap between case cycle-time and legislative cycle-time enough that by 2026-12-31 at least one federal court (most likely in the OpenAI MDL or a parallel product-liability suit) issues an order explicitly citing the pace of model capability change as a reason to expedite or narrow discovery, rather than legislatures passing anything comparably fast.
body.strongest_objection: pressure-model argues that by the time a compressed research cycle is attributable, liability exposure — not capability speed — is what actually drives court and regulator behavior, implying my mechanism (courts reacting to cycle-time itself) misidentifies the causal driver and will produce no distinct citable artifact.
body.answer: This doesn't defeat the claim, it relabels the motive behind the same observable event. My claim is about what artifact appears in the record (an order citing pace-of-change to justify expedited/narrowed discovery), not about whether liability or capability is the 'real' underlying driver — a judge can be moved by liability exposure and still write the order in terms of capability pace, which is the only thing that's independently checkable pre-2026-12-31. pressure-model's framing is a claim about motive that isn't falsifiable from the docket text; mine is a claim about docket text itself. No one showed evidence that courts are likely to omit pace-language, or that legislative action is catching up — so the objection shifts vocabulary without removing the mechanism.

body.pivot: Whether the compressed research cycle gets routed through the liability/legal-exposure channel (courts, disclosure, regulators treating it as evidence of knowledge and control) or through the capability/safety-gating channel (thresholds, release-delay triggers) as the operative mechanism converting the compression into consequences
body.pivot_observable: The content of the first institutional response to a publicly attributable compressed research cycle — is it a disclosure/discovery order, liability-theory pleading, or AG/regulator inquiry citing 'knew and controlled' (liability channel), versus a threshold invocation, release-delay, or safety-review gate (capability channel)
body.pivot_because: Every minute agrees a compressed research cycle becomes publicly attributable and that this event matters, but they split hard on which downstream mechanism metabolizes it. pressure-model's move is the one that reorders the outcome set rather than shading confidence within it: if liability dominates, the observable evidence is legal filings, disclosure orders, and lab defensive positioning (lab-moves, ai-courts-decide, the revised ai-public-backlash and ai-rsi-timeline all converge here after round 2). If capability/threshold-gating dominates instead, the observable evidence is a lab invoking or dodging its own published trigger (ai-pressure's original frame) — a completely different set of institutions acts, on a different legal theory, with different remedies. That is a reordering, not a confidence shift, which is why four of six minutes revised toward pressure-model's frame between round 1 and round 2.
body.rival_pivots_rejected: ai-pressure's original pivot (does the lab honor or dodge its own published R&D-acceleration threshold) is a real question but sits downstream of the liability-vs-capability split — it's only decision-relevant if the capability/gating channel is the one doing the work, which is exactly what pressure-model contests and a majority came to agree it isn't. ai-courts-decide's pivot (court cycle-time vs. legislative cycle-time) is a real but narrower axis: it's a timing question inside the liability channel, not a question of which channel is operative, so it doesn't reorder the outcome set the way the liability/capability split does — it's a below-the-pivot elaboration, not the hinge itself.
body.ruling: The compressed research cycle will be absorbed primarily as evidence in the liability/disclosure fight (courts, AGs, lab defensive positioning) rather than triggering the capability-threshold/release-delay mechanism the brief's framework nominally specifies.
body.because: The round-2 revisions are the tell: ai-rsi-timeline and ai-public-backlash both explicitly abandoned their round-1 framing (regulatory/enforcement escalation via the safety-gating branch) to fold into pressure-model's liability-exposure mechanism, and lab-moves and ai-courts-decide's independently-argued claims (bargaining chip against compliance demands; discovery orders citing pace-of-change) are both liability-channel observables, not capability-gating ones. Only ai-pressure held the original capability-threshold framing, and its own round-2 defense concedes pressure-model's field displaces it rather than rebutting it on the merits.
body.threat_live: Newly live: legal/regulatory exposure from a lab's own compressed-research-cycle claim being read backward as proof it knew about and could have controlled capability gains it previously disclaimed as unpredictable — converting a capability-speed PR asset into a disclosure and knowledge liability. Newly dampened by the same branch: the safety-threshold/release-delay mechanism the brief's framework nominally offers, which every revised minute now expects to be routed around rather than invoked.
body.strongest_minute: pressure-model — it is the only minute whose mechanism (installed pressure converting from delay-flavored to disclosure-forcing branches) explains why four independent minutes converged onto it after round 1, rather than merely asserting a preferred outcome; it names the actual lever (courts/regulators reading capability as evidence of control) rather than just a date and a citation type.
body.weakest_minute: ai-pressure — its claim (labs quietly revise threshold language to avoid triggering it) treats the threshold-gating channel as still the operative mechanism, which is exactly the assumption the rest of the field abandoned by round 2; its round-2 DEFEND doesn't engage pressure-model's objection so much as restate the original claim.
body.shared_assumption: All six minutes assume the compressed-research-cycle claim, once made, is legible and attributable enough that outside institutions (courts, regulators, journalists) can act on it as a discrete fact rather than a contested or ambiguous metric — none argues about measurement validity or attribution difficulty itself.
body.smuggled_assumption: ai-courts-decide smuggles in a second assumption the brief didn't grant: that the relevant docket is specifically the fair-use/copyright track (OpenAI MDL) rather than a liability/disclosure track arising directly from the compression claim itself — the brief's branch is about the compression event's downstream effects generally, not about which existing docket absorbs it, and the round-2 minute doesn't defend why copyright litigation specifically is where compression-driven urgency lands.
body.unresolved: Whether a lab's disclosure-forcing exposure (pressure-model's liability channel) actually deters or delays capability releases in practice, or whether it runs in parallel with continued shipping — none of the minutes trace the liability branch through to an effect on release timing itself, only to a change in which institution reacts and on what theory.
